section_title: What becomes of the beast and its armies?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 17 Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out in a loud voice to all the birds flying overhead, “Come, gather together for the great supper of God, 18 so that you may eat the flesh of kings and commanders and mighty men, of horses and riders, of everyone slave and free, small and great.”

19 Then I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies assembled to wage war against the One seated on the horse, and against His army. 20 But the beast was captured along with the false prophet, who on its behalf had performed signs deceiving those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. Both the beast and the false prophet were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur. 21 And the rest were killed with the sword that proceeded from the mouth of the One seated on the horse. And all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh.

context_lines: An angel calls the birds to a dreadful feast. Earlier in the chapter, people were blessed to be invited to the Lamb’s marriage supper. Here the invitation is to birds that will consume the defeated armies. Kings, commanders, mighty men, slaves and free people all appear in the announcement; rank cannot shield them from the outcome.

The beast and the kings gather to fight the rider and His army. John moves directly from that gathering to their defeat. The beast and the false prophet are captured, and the false prophet is identified by the signs that deceived people into receiving the beast’s mark and worshiping its image. This brings the deception of chapter 13 to its end.

The two are thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur. The rest of the assembled force are killed by the sword from the rider’s mouth, and the birds feed on their flesh. The scene ends with Christ’s victory. Chapter 20 will turn to the dragon, whose power stood behind the beast.
common_interpretation_lines: The main readings agree that the gathering against Christ fails and that the beast’s deceptive power cannot save it. The [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/revelation/19) connect the birds’ feast with Ezekiel 39 and emphasize the certainty of Christ’s victory. The imagery makes the defeat complete and public.

The identity of the defeated powers affects how teachers explain their end. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/), despite identifying the beast with Rome’s religious power in his wider reading, takes the beast and false prophet here as two men cast into punishment without first undergoing bodily death. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/19.htm) understands the pair as hostile civil and religious powers, particularly the papal order in his account of history. He reads their fate as the severe judgment of those powers and those who belong to them. These are the teachers’ particular identifications, rather than an agreed Christian identification of a present church or government.

The passage explicitly distinguishes the pair thrown alive into the lake from the remaining army killed by the sword. A proposed death, visit to the realm of the dead and resurrection of the pair before their casting is an added sequence; John does not describe those intervening events here.
god_plan_lines: The call to the birds closely parallels [Ezekiel 39:17–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ezekiel/39.htm): birds and beasts are summoned to feed on defeated warriors, horses and rulers, and God makes His judgment known among the nations. Revelation draws on that picture to show the overthrow of the beast’s assembled force. The connection in the imagery is clear even where readers differ over how the two prophecies fit on a timeline.

A related rescue appears in [2 Kings 19:14–19 and 32–36](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_kings/19.htm). Hezekiah brings an enemy’s threats before God, and the LORD delivers Jerusalem by striking the invading force. This is a parallel in God’s defense of His people and the failure of a seemingly overwhelming army, rather than a claim that the Assyrian invasion and Revelation’s battle are the same event.

[2 Thessalonians 2:8–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_thessalonians/2.htm) likewise joins deceptive signs, opposition to truth and the defeat of the lawless one by the Lord Jesus at His arrival. Together these passages direct attention to Christ’s authority over the forces that deceive and oppress.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
